schools.summary: Henry: the worst match ever made by the house of David — Jehoshaphat, grown greater but not wiser, joined with a degenerate idolater, whether from pride or from a policy of uniting the kingdoms.

Ellicott: 'riches and honour' repeated from 2 Chronicles 17:5; the affinity is Jehoram's marriage to Athaliah, and Ahab's seeking it proves Judah's prosperity; the vav is consecutive, not adversative.
Gill: the increasing riches and honour are the very thing that moved Ahab to court Jehoshaphat's friendship and affinity.
Clarke and Wesley: the affinity is Jehoram's marriage to Ahab's daughter Athaliah.

themes: the marriage of Jehoram and Athaliah

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil: the parallel's exact 'third year' (dated from the Syrian truce, cf. Jehoshaphat's 16th-17th year) is exchanged by the chronicler for the indefinite 'certain years'; the lavish feast is a deliberate plan, and 'persuaded' means 'incited/pricked on' (cf. 1 Chronicles 21:1).
Gill: the interval was two years (Syriac, Arabic), or the third year after the affinity was contracted.

themes: the royal banquet as a snare

schools.summary: Ellicott: essentially 1 Kings 22:4, from which the narratives coincide; 'Ramoth' means 'heights'; the chronicler disturbs the older symmetry to make Jehoshaphat's assent more definite. Keil sets the exchange at the head of the consultation.
Clarke: Ramoth-gilead belonged to Israel but was held by Syria; the whole chapter is explained on 1 Kings 22.
Henry: 'I am as thou art' — some men's kindnesses are dangerous; Ahab begs help to recover a city that was Jehoshaphat's by right, his own title being usurped.
Henry: the great duty of acknowledging God and enquiring at his word before we undertake anything — yet also the great danger of bad company, into which even a good man like Jehoshaphat is drawn.
Wesley: enquiry is made by particular believing prayer, unbiased consulting of Scripture and conscience, and a close regard to the hints of providence.
Ellicott: the words stand exactly as 1 Kings 22:5; 'enquire at the word' is better 'seek the word.'

themes: enquiring at the word of the LORD

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'the prophets' (the king's establishment); the chronicler rounds Kings' 'about four hundred' and writes Adonai, not ha-elohim, quietly withholding the covenant name from these court-prophets.
Henry: the misery of a man surrounded by flatterers and flattering prophets who cry peace — Ahab was cheated into his ruin, preferring those who humoured him to the one who warned him.
Clarke: they consult the prophets about the war, and all except Micaiah promise victory.
Ellicott: the chronicler opens with 'and' for 'but,' standing exactly as the literal Hebrew of 1 Kings 22:7; by asking for a prophet 'besides,' Jehoshaphat tacitly disowns the whole assembly.
Henry: Jehoshaphat's discernment — unable to rest in smooth assurances, he wanted the fair warning of a true prophet rather than the humouring of false ones.

themes: a prophet of the LORD besides

schools.summary: Ellicott: the chronicler aggravates the opposition, 'all his days for evil'; Micaiah = 'Who is like Iah?' (the oldest form of the Name), Imla = 'he is full'; 'let not the king say so' deprecates an omen of evil.
Henry: Jehoshaphat could scarcely find heart for even a mild rebuke of Ahab's hatred of the prophet; Ahab's complaint that Micaiah never prophesies good is in truth his highest commendation.
Ellicott: 'called for one of his officers' is literally 'called to a eunuch' (cf. 1 Chronicles 28:1); the name appears in the contracted form Mikahu, for which the margin gives the usual spelling.

Ellicott: 'were sitting each on his throne'; 'clothed in their robes' lacks the needed pronoun (Syriac 'raiment spotted white and black'); 'void place' = threshing-floor, the word perhaps corrupt from beruddim, 'spotted'; 'were prophesying.'
Clarke: the Targum's gloss — Ahab consulted false prophets, but Jehoshaphat sought the LORD and prayed at the entering in of Samaria, and before them the false prophets prophesied lies.
Ellicott: 'push' is properly 'butt,' the goring of a horned beast (Daniel 8:4; figuratively Deuteronomy 33:17); 'until they be consumed' = 'unto destroying them,' a promise of total victory.

Ellicott: 'prophesied' is nibbe'im, while v.9's mithnabbe'im can mean 'raving' (Jeremiah 29:26); the nabi is the spokesman/herald of God (Assyrian nabu, the god Nebo); 'and prosper' = 'thou shalt prosper' (cf. Genesis 20:7).
Clarke: all save Micaiah promise Ahab victory.
Henry: a king cheated by smooth unanimity was cheated to his ruin, preferring the humourers to the one who warned him.
Ellicott: 'with one assent' is literally 'one mouth' (cf. Joshua 9:2); better read 'the prophets have with one mouth spoken good'; 'like one of theirs' answers Kings' 'like the word of one of them.'
Ellicott: 'even' is better 'nay, but' — a flat refusal of the messenger's plea; and the chronicler writes 'my God' where Kings has 'Jehovah,' a personal allegiance the four hundred had forfeited.

themes: 'what my God saith, that will I speak'

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'shall I forbear' (Kings 'shall we'); the chronicler gives a definite reply that 'they' (the Syrians) shall be delivered up, recalling the Delphic oracle to Croesus — though Micaiah's mockery is transparent enough.

Ellicott: the verse stands word for word as 1 Kings 22:16; 'I adjure thee' is the same solemn charge the high priest laid upon Christ (Matthew 26:63) — a truthful witness bound by God's name to speak a truth that will condemn him.
Ellicott: 'upon the mountains' (Kings 'unto'); 'as sheep' is 'like the flock,' of sheep and goats — a scattered, shepherdless flock is an army without its king, and the true oracle of defeat.
Ellicott: 'but evil' as in Kings, with a marginal variation, referring back to the king's complaint at v.7 — Ahab hears the true oracle only as confirmation of his grudge against the prophet.

themes: the message hated with the messenger

schools.summary: Ellicott: the chronicler's connectives and abridgement ('hear ye' for 'hear thou'; the shortened host of heaven); the Vulgate renders 'therefore hear the word of the LORD' — the true throne set over the thrones of Samaria.

themes: the true court above the kings

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'one said thus, and another said thus' — the heavenly council debating; the text is certainly right against those who would smooth away a scene that shows Ahab's ruin decreed and the deception permitted within God's government.
Ellicott: render 'and the spirit came forth' — with the article, a single volunteer stepping out of the host to take the commission the LORD had invited.

Clarke: the Targum's gloss names the enticing spirit and bars it from returning among the righteous, since one who speaks falsely may keep no mansion there — a curiosity, but resting on the plain sense that the deception was proposed and permitted before God.

outliers.note: Preserves the Targum's fancy that the enticing spirit came forth from the abode of the righteous, offered itself as a spirit of false prophecy, and was then barred from returning among the righteous for having spoken falsely.

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'become a spirit of falsehood'; Scripture shows God overruling and even sending deception as judgment (Isaiah 19:14; Ezekiel 14:9; 2 Thessalonians 2:11), the verb pittah ('entice/deceive') running through the vision.

Henry: two doctrines — the power of Satan by divine permission (one lying spirit makes four hundred), and the justice of God in giving up to strong delusion those who will not receive the love of the truth.

themes: a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths
God permits but does not author the lie

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'and now' for 'now therefore,' 'these thy prophets' where Kings and several MSS read 'all these' — Micaiah brings the whole vision down on Ahab with a 'therefore.'
Wesley: 'See the power of Satan! One lying spirit can make four hundred lying prophets,' becoming a murderer by being a liar and destroying men by deceiving them.

themes: 'the LORD hath put a lying spirit'

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'smote' is the chronicler's shortened form; the taunt is literally 'where is the way the Spirit of Jehovah passed to speak with thee?' — a mockery that unwittingly concedes the true word came through the one, not the four hundred.

Ellicott: 'destined to see' on the day of hiding, in 'a chamber within a chamber'; that Zedekiah's later history is unrecorded shows (with Ewald) the original narrative was much fuller than this extract.
Henry: the persecutor is 'made to see in that day' what he will not now believe; the day always comes that declares who was right and who wrong.
Ellicott: the chronicler addresses several attendants ('take ye') where Kings has one; 'governor' is sar, a prefect over the city; 'carry back' is literally 'make him return' to custody.

Ellicott: 'of affliction' (lahats) is accusative — 'bread with stint, water with stint,' literally 'squeezing' (cf. Isaiah 30:20); 'until I return in peace' is the chronicler's correction of 'until I come.'

Wesley: 'this fellow' — the faithful minister's frequent lot, hated for being true to God; yet that day will declare who is right, to the consolation of the persecuted and the confusion of the persecutors.

Ellicott: the words of 1 Kings 22:28; Micaiah makes the bystanders witnesses; 'Hearken, all ye people' opens the book of Micah (Micah 1:2), and (with Thenius) the section bears marks of historical truth, likely from Jehu son of Hanani's history (2 Chronicles 20:34).
Henry: the persecuted may appeal to the issue, as Micaiah does; the day will declare who is in the right and who in the wrong.

themes: 'if thou return, the LORD hath not spoken by me'
the prophet stakes all on the event

schools.summary: Henry: Jehoshaphat will be endangered in his robes yet delivered, Ahab disguised yet slain — no art or arms can save those God has appointed to ruin, nor any danger destroy those he will protect.
Clarke: both kings go up against the Syrians, the confederate armies are defeated, and the king of Israel is slain.

themes: the word about to be proved

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'disguising myself and entering!' is a hurried, exclamatory idiom; 'they went' is the chronicler's reading where Kings has 'he' (Ahab) went into the battle.
Clarke: refers the disguise to his fuller treatment at 1 Kings 22:30.
Henry: in urging Jehoshaphat to keep his robes Ahab really aimed at his ally's life — unprincipled treachery, justly requited when the disguise failed to save Ahab himself.

Ellicott: Kings numbers the chariot-captains as 'thirty and two' (from the earlier Syrian wars, 1 Kings 20), which the chronicler passes over; the Syrian order to spare all but the king of Israel concentrates the whole force on Ahab alone.

Ellicott: 'the LORD helped him, and God moved them from him' is the chronicler's own addition, reading the cry as a cry to God; a perfectly natural event (the captains discovering their mistake) is rightly regarded as providential, for Hebrew faith knows no order of the world apart from the constant activity of Jehovah.
Clarke gives the Targum ('the Word of the LORD brought him assistance'); Wesley: the cry — to friends, to enemies, or to God — was not in vain, for an invisible power moved the captains to depart.
Henry: Jehoshaphat cried to God and was heard, the LORD moving the captains to depart — God has all men's hearts in his hand and turns them against their own first intentions.

Ellicott: 'at a venture' means without design (cf. 2 Samuel 15:11; Rashi: 'without knowing why he chose that man'); the wound fell at the one opening of the breastplate, where the versions only guess at the armour's anatomy.
Clarke: the Targum names the archer a Syrian captain and reads the random shot as the appointed fulfilment of the prophecies spoken against Ahab, the arrow finding the seam of the mail.

Ellicott: 'increased' = 'grew' (cf. Genesis 40:10); Ahab 'continued holding himself up in the chariot' — the chronicler's preferable reading; and the sequel (1 Kings 22:36-38) is omitted because Jehoshaphat had no part in it and the true climax is the king's death at sundown.
Clarke: real courage and patriotism in Ahab's holding himself up lest his troops give way; and the standing truth that God is represented as doing what in his providence he only permits.

themes: the dying king upright in his chariot
God permits what he is said to do
